Baram v0.7.4 opens the app up to themes and editor plugins written by other people, and
fixes a way a document could be quietly damaged by autosave.

If you are updating from v0.7.3 and want the short version: **check the first bug fix
below** — an image on a line with text could be rewritten as escaped characters when the
file autosaved.

---

# New and improved

## Themes can come from somewhere other than Baram

Until now the only themes you had were the eight built into the app. Settings › Appearance
has a new **Browse Themes** screen: search a registry, read what you are agreeing to,
install, and the theme applies without a restart and is still there after one. An installed
theme shows an update badge when a newer version is listed, and a theme withdrawn as
malicious is switched off for you, with the app falling back to following your system
appearance.

**No themes are published yet.** The registry has none today, so the browse screen will
tell you it is empty. The screen ships now so that the first published theme has somewhere
to arrive; browsing, installing, updating and revocation have so far been exercised against
test fixtures rather than a live entry.

A theme is somebody else's CSS running inside your document, so installing one puts it
through a pipeline before it can touch anything: remote URLs and `@import` are refused
outright, bundled images are inlined so there is no address left to fetch, `!important` is
stripped, and the whole sheet is re-checked every time it is applied rather than only at
install — the stored file is a file on your disk, and anything could have edited it since.
The consent dialog is rendered inside a shadow tree so no theme's stylesheet can reach it
to hide or repaint the thing you are using to decide.

## A theme can carry both a light and a dark palette

A theme used to be one palette. It can now carry a light one and a dark one and follow your
system, so the colours change at sunset without you picking a different theme.

## Your theme can leave the app

- **HTML and PDF exports can carry your active theme's palette.** The export dialog has a
  new choice: Baram's default look, or your theme's colours. Default output is byte-for-byte
  what it was. If your theme is dark, the dialog warns you that the PDF will print a dark
  background.
- **The Theme Editor can export a theme as an installable package.** Fill in author,
  description, licence and version and you get a `.zip` in the shape Baram's own installer
  reads. Note that installing one is a registry operation today: there is no
  install-from-file button yet, so a package you export is for publishing, not for handing
  to a friend.

## The page itself has dials, and each one says where its value came from

Settings › Editor has **Line width** and **Editor padding** as dials you can drag, and they
are the visible half of something larger. An appearance value is now merged from three
layers — Baram's default, your theme, and your own setting — and the app keeps track of
which layer won. Each dial shows that alongside its value (Default / Theme / Custom) and
has its own revert, so you can put one item back without touching the rest.

Two layout values no stylesheet could reach — the editor's width and the sidebar's width —
were written as inline styles, which beat any CSS. They travel through a variable channel
now, which is what will let a theme or a dial reach them at all.

A dial you have not touched writes nothing at all and leaves the value to the stylesheet,
which is deliberate: pinning defaults inline would override rules that are meant to win,
including the one that lets a system-following theme change at sunset.

## Plugins can draw inside the editor

A plugin manifest could declare `tiptapExtensions` before this release; the field validated
and the plugin loaded, and then nothing happened, because nothing in the app read it. It is
wired now. A plugin can contribute decorations, key handlers, input rules and paste rules to
every editing surface — the main editor, the background editors that keep your other tabs
warm, and quick capture — and the install consent screen shows a new `extensions` permission
when one does.

The registry could not list such a plugin either: publishing refused anything that was not
sandboxed, and a plugin that draws in the editor cannot be sandboxed — a sandboxed plugin
lives in its own webview and has no way to hand the editor a ProseMirror object. The first
one is now published: **Bullet Threading**, which draws the outline path from the outermost
ancestor list item down to the one holding your caret.

- **You can read a plugin's README before you install it.** It used to be inside the
  archive, which meant deciding whether to grant full trust and then installing the plugin
  to find out what it was.
- **Plugin settings can say more.** Numbers can carry a range, and there are colour fields
  (which offer your theme's own colours) and dropdowns with named options.

---

# Fixed

## An image on the same line as text no longer eats itself

If you wrote `Logo: ![logo](url)` — an image on a line with other text — putting the cursor
in it and saving rewrote that line on disk as escaped characters:
`!\[logo]\(https\://…)`. The picture was gone and the markdown was set in plain text. One
autosave tick was enough; you did not have to save deliberately.

An image on a line with text is not valid in Baram's document schema, and the loader
allowed it anyway. The syntax-reveal machinery that unfolds an image into its markdown then
split the surrounding paragraph, lost track of the closing bracket, and could not fold it
back. Such an image is now drawn and selectable but does not unfold — edit its markdown in
source mode (`Cmd/Ctrl+/`). An image on a line of its own is unchanged.

## Backlinks and rename read your note the way the editor does

Baram's link index found `[[links]]` and `((block#^refs))` by scanning each line with a
pattern, which meant it counted the ones you wrote inside a code fence, a code span, raw
HTML, a maths block, an image's alt text or a link definition. The editor does not read
those as links. Two things followed: your backlinks panel and graph showed examples out of
your code blocks, and renaming a file or a block ID **silently rewrote the example text
inside them** — and the same rename produced different bytes depending on whether you did it
from the editor, from source mode, or with the tab closed. All of those now share one answer
to "is this prose?", and it is the editor's.

- **Renaming a block ID trusted a line number it had remembered.** If the referring file
  changed outside Baram while its tab was closed — another editor, `git pull`, a sync client
  — the reference had moved down a line, the rewrite matched nothing, and it reported
  success. Your definition became `^b2` and every link to it stayed `^b1`, with nothing
  said. Rename now reads each referring file as it stands, and any file it cannot fix is
  reported to you instead of passed over.
- **Tags on the graph were cut at the first hyphen** — `#deep-work` drew as `deep`, while
  the tag panel showed the whole thing.
- **A file saved with old Mac line endings had its fences read inside-out**, so a rename
  edited the examples in the fence and missed the references outside it.
- **A note's own front matter is no longer indexed for block references.** Nothing ever
  renamed them, so they sat in your backlinks pointing at an id that had moved on.

## Renaming a folder works on Windows

On Windows, renaming a folder in the file tree failed four ways at once. The frontend split
the path on `/` only, so `C:\vault\ns` came out as the folder's name and the new path it
built was rejected as outside the vault — the rename never reached the code that moves
files. Past that point the backend compared paths joined with `\` against a `/` prefix, so
it reported zero files moved and listed every note it had just moved as unverified. Relative
links from notes outside the folder were resolved by a routine that split on `/` too, so a
`..` swallowed the entire drive path and no such link was updated. And your open tabs and
the file cache stayed pointed at the old path, so a tab with unsaved changes could save to a
location that no longer existed. macOS and Linux are unchanged.

## Exports

- **Word and EPUB decide which images to embed from what Pandoc actually reads.** The
  judgement used to run on the parser's interpreted text and on only a few kinds of node, so
  images Pandoc treats as raw HTML were staged anyway — spending one of the 256 slots — and
  images Pandoc does render were sometimes dropped with no notice. A note with thousands of
  unclosed raw environments took 3.5 seconds to scan; it now takes 17 milliseconds.
- **A highlight, formula or subscript that wrapped a code span came out literal.** The
  converter took the first closing delimiter it found, and if that one was inside code it
  rejected the match and consumed it, missing the real closer further along. Delimiters now
  pair the way the editor pairs them. A megabyte of heavily marked-up notes exports in 0.19
  seconds instead of 8.2.
- **Notion exports no longer rewrite your file paths and URLs.** A `~` in a path, a `$` in a
  query string or a `^` in a tag was being treated as a mark and replaced, which broke the
  address. The Pandoc path had this guard already; Notion has it now.
- **A note saved with Windows or old-Mac line endings** had its first code fence never
  close, so everything after it was left untouched by every converter.
- **The PDF export's theme argument used to control nothing at all** — the receiving end
  discarded it. It is replaced by one that carries the actual palette.

## Plugins

- **Installing an editor plugin did nothing.** The installer skipped loading any plugin that
  declared editor extensions — no error and no "restart required". If you have one installed
  and dead, toggling Enabled off and on still works; this build makes the install itself
  work.
- **Switching tabs dropped the plugin.** The restored tab brought back its own plugin list
  from whenever it was cached.
- **A trusted plugin was never told its settings changed**, so your edits took effect only
  after a reload. The documentation and the API comment both said otherwise.
- **Two withdrawn plugins showed two "Remove" buttons a screen reader could not tell apart.**
  Each now reads "Remove {name}".

## Appearance

- **Switching your OS between light and dark left open code blocks highlighted in the old
  scheme.** The editor watched a store field that a paired theme never changes, so the
  condition was never true. Code blocks and source mode now follow the switch, without
  rebuilding the editor underneath your cursor.
- **Changing your OS appearance while the Theme Editor was open wiped your live preview.**
  The editor now holds the preview while it is open.

---

**Updating.** Every platform installs in place and restarts — press **Install & Restart** in
the update dialog. Linux `.deb` and `.rpm` cannot be updated in place by the updater; those,
and any install that fails, open the releases page instead.
